en: The Sutra of the Samādhi of the Ultimate Treasure, Scroll One.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, together with twelve hundred [monks].
There were fifty bhikṣus together with ninety billion bodhisattvas, all of whom were like Mañjuśrī.

At that time, all around the four sides of the Bamboo Grove, the earth naturally produced *mandārava* flowers of various wondrous colors never seen before in the world; each flower had a million petals, and upon each flower sat a Buddha. Above each Buddha was a jeweled canopy with interlaced lattices, and from within the canopies issued the sounds of musical instruments.
Before each Buddha sat a bodhisattva, all like Mañjuśrī, seated and inquiring about the Dharma.
The site of the Bamboo Garden was as level as the buddha-field of Trāyastriṃśa;
the light of the sun and moon throughout the great trichiliocosm was entirely eclipsed, and no radiance remained.

Within these hundred days, they saw only the Buddhas; all the great hells found rest. The various birds and beasts neither drank nor ate, yet all partook of the flavor of the Dharma and remained peaceful for a hundred days; beholding the Buddha with joy, they forgot their hunger.

All the people universally attained the flavor of the Dharma; for a hundred days they were secure and free from thoughts of food or drink, their minds delighted as they gave rise to the unsurpassed resolve. All the trees produced sounds.

Within the Bamboo Grove, a bathing pool was manifested by transformation; within the pool grew a hundred thousand varieties of flowers, and upon each flower was a lion throne covered with a lattice of jewels. Upon each throne sat a bodhisattva, with celestial beings standing in attendance at their sides. Within the canopies, there were ten thousand kinds of musical instruments for each. Withered trees a thousand years old all sprouted flowers and leaves, and all the trees leaned toward one another. Among those women on the left and right of the Bamboo Grove who beheld the Buddha, they were all transformed into men; they were no longer subject to desire and all attained the Dharma-eye.

At that time, the Buddha entered the Treasure Tathāgata Samādhi, causing all ninety trillion lands to tremble throughout the four cardinal directions, the four intermediate directions, and the zenith and nadir across infinite Buddha-fields. Each of these fields dispatched a bodhisattva bearing exquisite flowers to come to the Bamboo Grove to pay homage and make offerings; having completed these rites, they each withdrew to sit aside.
Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Kings, and the gods of the desire realm, each accompanied by their retinues, made offerings in the air with celestial flowers, incense, and music;

likewise, the great nāga kings, asura kings, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, and others, each with their own countless subordinates, came to where the Buddha was to pay homage, serve, and make offerings.
Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying,
"What auspicious omen is this that has now been manifested?
The Buddha said:
"The response that is without responding is the true response.
Śāriputra asked: "What is the meaning of 'the response that is without responding'?"
The Buddha said, "Go and ask the Bodhisattva Ratnākara; he shall explain this meaning for you.
Thereupon, Śāriputra asked Ratnākara:
"What omen does this present agitation portend?
Bodhisattva Ratnamati replied to Śāriputra:
"Is it because your doubts as an Arhat are so heavy that you have not yet understood?"
To have perceptions and conceptions is not the way to reach exhaustion; the absence of perception and the absence of volitional action is the Treasure of the Dharma.

Long ago, when I first resolved my mind and sought the path of a Bodhisattva together with thirty-six billion people, Śākyamuni was also among them. All that they aspired to involved arising and ceasing; all dharmas are fundamentally empty, like a mirage. To give rise to perceptions and volitional actions, to hold fast to these constructed dharmas, and to seek through the extinction of practice for the sake of desire and conceptualization—claiming to have attained the Way—is the root of sin. Such arising of perceptions destroys all wisdom. Seeking the Three Honored Ones while perceiving Nirvāṇa as something to be grasped, one’s doubts are not exhausted, and though the body may perish, birth and death continue without end.

When an Arhat attains Nirvana, it is like a sleeping person whose body remains on the bed; for a time they rest, yet life does not depart from the body. Because the Arhat has attained dhyāna, this constitutes a great doubt.
Ratnākara further asked Śāriputra:

“For example, when a dragon king raises clouds and rain, they gather from all four directions until it is dark and one knows not whence they come. From the ninth stage downward, a bodhisattva has already attained sixty thousand samādhis; since their manifestations are inherently limitless, why should there be any further doubt as to where they come from?”

Śāriputra said: "Because I failed to find a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra) while studying, my root of doubt has remained unsevered; now that I have heard your honored Dharma, there is nothing further for me to gain."
It is like a person playing music for a hundred birds; though the music is harmonious and exquisite, the birds do not listen or receive it.
Now I am likewise unable to understand this Dharma, yet all newly initiated bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, upon hearing of the immeasurable and sublime merit of this samādhi, [will surely embrace it].
It is like seeing the light of a fire for a brief moment at night; once the fire has extinguished, there is only the old darkness and nothing to be seen.
Now I am likewise of no benefit.

I vow to kindle a fire eight thousand *li* in size and cast my body into its midst, remaining there for billions of eons before emerging. Even if I must again enter the three evil realms to be devoured by all manner of beings, and only after thousands of billions of eons am reborn as a human, would it still be possible for me to find a virtuous friend?
Ratnākara replied:

"Although fire is vast, it cannot burn the defilements of the mind; one who studies without *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and does not encounter a *kalyāṇamitra* (virtuous friend) shall not attain *sarvajñatā* (omniscience)."
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama addressed the Buddha, saying:
“All dharmas have no master; who is it that accomplishes sarvajñatā?
Who is it that attains perfect enlightenment?”
“Disciples and pratyekabuddhas, please bestow your great grace upon us by expounding the meaning of this.
The Buddha said, “Excellent!”
Your question is profound and subtle; you wish to sever the very root of birth and death.
I shall now explain it for you—listen attentively and receive it.
If a son or daughter of good family wishes to attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, they should practice the nine treasures of the Dharma:

First, seeing that the various heavens have no abode and exist as names alone; second, seeing that the people of the world exist as mere characters alone; third, seeing that the suffering of the five realms of existence consists of nothing but habitual tendencies alone; fourth, seeing that earth, water, fire, and wind are fundamentally empty; fifth, seeing that the future, past, and present are like plantain trees, devoid of thought; sixth, observing that the present cycle of birth and death has no fundamental limit; seventh, contemplating that all samādhis are tranquil and without coming or going; eighth, observing that throughout the great trichiliocosm of Buddha-fields, there is ultimately no one who attains samādhi; ninth, seeing all wriggling creatures within the great trichiliocosm and desiring to deliver them all so that they may become equal to the Buddhas—these are the nine jewels.
"One who attains this notion of non-action can decisively sever all great notions.
Ratna-āgata asked again:
"Since all dharmas are without notion, how should one abide so as to attain non-abiding?"
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas have no abiding; to abide is to conceptualize. A thought that does not arise is neither conceptualization nor the Path—it too is conceptualization.
By severing the seeking for non-conceptualization, one attains abiding in non-abiding."
Ratnākara asked again:
"By what conditions should one cross over the various desires?
The Buddha said:
"All desires are stainless, without measure, without master, without going, and without coming; they are like space, equal to nirvana, and equal to the nameless.
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama said:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"It is so profound and wondrous!
Bodhisattva Paṃśi addressed the Buddha, saying:

"If a bodhisattva wishes to sit beneath the tree of enlightenment, adorn the buddha-field, and instruct those in the ten directions, making all buddha-fields like this Bamboo Garden, and universally cause them to attain the state of non-arising—by practicing what dharma can one achieve this?"

The Buddha said: “One should practice the eight forms of rectitude: first, rectitude regarding the resonance of the nameless; second, rectitude regarding the sound of the nameless; third, rectitude in observing that the Buddha-lands of the ten directions are equal and without duality; fourth, rectitude in seeing that the dharmas of the great trichiliocosm are equal and without difference; fifth, rectitude in observing all things in the ten directions and desiring to make them equal to the Buddha; sixth, rectitude in seeing within formlessness that all things have neither arising nor ceasing; seventh, rectitude in seeing the entry into various samādhis without any thought of coming, going, or mutual response; eighth, rectitude in seeing that the parinirvāṇa or non-parinirvāṇa of the Buddhas of the ten directions is likewise equal and without difference. These are the eight dharmas.”

“From this, Bodhisattvas will swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), and their instruction of those in the ten directions will become like that of the Bamboo Grove.
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama again addressed the Buddha, saying:

“Now these superior persons have each come from afar; beholding the World-Honored One, they were so filled with joy that they forgot to eat. That they have now encountered and heard of this sublime samādhi—is this not brought about by the fundamental vows and past merits of their former lives?”
The Buddha said:

“It is neither my original vow, nor am I apart from my original vow. My practice is always diligent, I do not lose any of the samādhis, I constantly follow good spiritual friends, and I remain far removed from worldly affairs. Being tranquil and seldom attending assemblies, my mind is set solely upon samādhi; it is for this reason that I have now come to rain down precious jewels upon this great assembly.”
Ratnākara asked again:
“If a bodhisattva who has newly resolved to attain awakening wishes to practice this samādhi, how should they practice so as to achieve it?
The Buddha said:
"One should practice eight dharmas to attain this samādhi:
first, to attain this samādhi in the very presence of the Buddha;

second, to make offerings to the arhats and true persons of the ten directions, practicing the bodhisattva path for billions of kalpas without slackening, and upon hearing this honored dharma of samādhi all at once, to explain it, draw near to it, and uphold it without ever departing from it."

Third, although one may fill the world with stupas by making offerings to the *śarīra* and plant merit without deficiency, this does not benefit the Dharma; if at that time one turns the mind toward practice, one immediately enters the gate of wisdom.
Fourth, although one may attain the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), one cannot thereby distance oneself from birth and death throughout the ten directions.

Fifth, when a bodhisattva sees the suffering of the five destinies and desires to deliver them, they would risk their own life to provide rescue without regarding it as a hardship, further desiring to lead those beings to peace and the state of Buddhahood.

Sixth, the Bodhisattva serves people as a slave serves his master or a noble; he desires to deliver them without weariness or hardship. Why is this? Because he knows they are fundamentally non-existent (*mūla-abhāva*).
Seventh, the Bodhisattva observes the ninety-six kinds of paths and, within them, realizes the arising of the Dharma and its abiding.

Eighth, to practice the six *pāramitās* and make offerings to the community of *bhikṣus* for even billions of *kalpas* is not equal to hearing this samādhi for a single moment. For those throughout the ten directions who are destined to become Buddhas, what shall they take as their proof?

Upon hearing this samādhi, one immediately knows that such a person has attained the realization of Buddhahood. Should anyone give rise to the aspiration for this samādhi, and with joy, faith, and delight, understand its wisdom, they shall have already realized sixty thousand samādhis; this constitutes the eighth jewel of the Dharma.
"By practicing this samādhi, one immediately attains the gates of dhāraṇī.
At that time, the Buddha smiled with joy; his radiance was brilliant and magnificent, illuminating everywhere without exception.
Mañjuśrī bowed his head to the Buddha and said, “The Buddha does not smile without cause; there must be an intention behind this smile.
The Buddha spoke to Mañjuśrī:

"It is exactly as you have said. This Bodhisattva Ratnāgama has come from the buddha-field of the Tathāgata Ratna. It is nine hundred million buddha-lands away from here; that field is named Svabhāvasarvadharma. Any sons or daughters of good family who are born there do not emerge from a womb; they undergo no further suffering and are free from affectionate attachments. They are all born within natural flowers and fragrances, and upon birth, they stand upright without needing nursing. They naturally enjoy music morning and evening, remaining in tranquil purity as their Dharma and Sangha."

If good sons or good daughters hear of this samādhi, they shall immediately eliminate the sins of six million four hundred thousand kalpas; when their sins are exhausted and their lives end, they will attain rebirth in that land.

In the realm of the Tathāgata Ratna, there is no light from the sun or moon; although the sun and moon exist, their brilliance is obscured and they do not appear. However, if a person is to be reborn there, the sun, moon, and stars will immediately manifest. Those who see the radiance of the sun, moon, and stars know that someone is about to be reborn there.
Yet the śrāvakas do not perceive or know this; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and bodhisattvas with supernormal powers can see and know it. For this reason, I have smiled now.
The worthy Subhūti and Śāriputra both stepped forward, prostrated themselves, and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"We pray that you will bestow upon us great grace and empower us with your majestic spiritual power, so that we may reach that land, the realm where all phenomena are spontaneous, to pay our respects and make offerings there, and then return in a mere moment."
The Buddha immediately granted permission for them to go, and they all arrived in that land.

Upon arriving, they saw everything contained therein; there was likewise a city of Rājagṛha and a Bamboo Grove, and everything belonging to Śākyamuni Buddha was exactly like this, without any difference.
Śāriputra asked Subhūti: "Did the Tathāgata follow me?
Having finished their rites of salutation and service, Subhūti and Śāriputra returned from there; when they arrived at the assembly, it was seen to be exactly as it had been before.
The Buddha asked Śāriputra,
"When you arrived in that land just now, what did you see? He replied:
"I see that country as being exactly like this one.
The merits of the Buddhas are most sublime, most sublime; how fortunate are those gathered here who have been able to behold this!"
The Bodhisattva Samiti rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and expressed his wish to ask a question:
"Does the dharma of non-arising possess conceptualization, or is it without conceptualization?"
Does the unarisen thought exist or not?
Is Nirvana, in its profound stillness, existent or non-existent?
Does that which does not arise have form or not?
"If there were no form, yet one were to exist within that intermediate state, who would be the master of the five paths of birth and death?

The Buddha said, "All dharmas are fundamentally non-existent and entirely pure; because of the arising and ceasing of causes and conditions, all dharmas are produced. Since emptiness creates emptiness, there is fundamentally no such master."

When the Bodhisattva Samiti heard what the Buddha had said, eighty-six thousand devas and humans all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). They ascended into the air to a height of one hundred and sixty *zhang* above the ground, then descended from above and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet.
At that time, the earth of this trichiliocosm shook with great intensity, and Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What auspicious omen is this earthquake that has just occurred?"
The Buddha told Maitreya:

"The shaking of the earth is not limited to this alone; the lands throughout the ten directions are also universally shaken. In each of those lands, there are likewise eighty-six thousand gods and humans who have attained the state of non-arising and dwell in mid-air, all exactly as it is here."
Maitreya asked again:
"How does a bodhisattva attain the patient endurance of the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti)?
The Buddha said:
“There are six dharmas by which one attains this:

First, knowing those among gods and humans who are destined to attain Buddhahood but have not yet received their prediction (*vyākaraṇa*), I shall go and grant them that prediction, without sharing this knowledge with the people of the worlds throughout the ten directions.

Second, within the great trichiliocosm, if there are sons or daughters of good family who are destined to attain Buddhahood but have not yet received their prediction, I shall go and grant them that prediction, without sharing this knowledge with the people of the worlds throughout the ten directions.”

Third, regarding those among the inhabitants of the various hells who are destined to attain Buddhahood, I shall go to all of them to bestow their predictions (vyākaraṇa), yet I shall not share this knowledge with the people of the worlds throughout the ten directions;

fourth, I shall know the places of rebirth for all beings throughout the ten directions after they have ended their lives, yet I shall not share this knowledge with the people of the worlds throughout the ten directions;

fifth, I shall know the exhaustion of the life-span of all people throughout the worlds of the ten directions, yet I shall not share this knowledge with the people of the worlds throughout the ten directions.

Sixth, I fully know whether the Buddhas of the ten directions enter parinirvāṇa or do not enter parinirvāṇa, yet I do not share this knowledge with the people of the world in the ten directions; this is the sixth dharma for swiftly attaining the patience regarding the non-arising of all phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"This samādhi is supremely great and honored; desiring that the entire assembly may universally attain it, what dharma should be practiced so that they may obtain it?"

The Buddha said: “One should practice nine dharmas: first, viewing all dharmas as entirely pure and boundless; second, viewing all devas as also entirely pure and boundless; third, viewing all births and deaths as entirely pure and boundless; fourth, viewing the five destinies as entirely pure; fifth, seeking nothing within desire and being entirely pure therein; sixth, viewing all forms within the three realms as entirely pure and boundless; seventh, viewing nirvāṇa as entirely pure and boundless; eighth, contemplating the hells as entirely pure and boundless; ninth, seeing that throughout the ten directions there is no one who can be named. These are the nine dharmas. If a bodhisattva practices in this way, they will swiftly attain this samādhi.”
Maitreya addressed the Buddha, saying:
"When a bodhisattva attains sixty thousand samādhis, do these samādhis have limits or not?
Is the attainment of these sixty thousand samādhis considered to be without limit?"
The Buddha said:
"Although you have attained sixty thousand samādhis, they are merely names; you cannot yet exhaustively fulfill all samādhis.
Furthermore, samādhi is not of only one kind; there is the samādhi of non-thought and the samādhi of detachment from desire."
There is the samādhi of sitting and listening to the Buddhas of the ten directions; there is the samādhi of adorning the buddha-fields where flowers and incense arrive spontaneously;
there is the samādhi whereby all people who hear the Dharma preached attain their original nature;
there is the samādhi of emerging from all dharmas without returning to conceptualization; and there is the samādhi of transforming into a hundred kinds of sounds when preaching the sūtras.
There is the Samādhi of the Natural Fragrance of Flowers in Billions of Buddha-lands; there is the Samādhi of Subduing All Multitudes of Sentient Beings;
there is the Samādhi of Arousing the Lion’s Intent to Walk Alone and Stride Unhindered;
there is the Samādhi wherein wherever one looks, all are inspired toward Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi; and there is the Samādhi wherein wherever one dwells, none [fail to...]
There is the samādhi of not making offerings; the samādhi where, when a turbulent wind arises, it is like the sound of the Buddha preaching the sūtras;
the samādhi where whichever gate one faces remains unopened; the samādhi where lions appear wherever one is;
the samādhi of flying to the ten directions; and the samādhi where, as one approaches a gate, it does not remain unopened and bodhisattvas from the ten directions arrive.

There is the Samādhi of Coming from the Infinite; there is the Samādhi of Sitting and Knowing the Minds of People in the Ten Directions; there is the Samādhi of Destroying and Extinguishing All Perceptions;
there is the Samādhi of Destroying and Extinguishing All Consciousnesses; there is the Samādhi of Unifying all Buddha-lands of the Ten Directions into a Single Land;
there is the Samādhi of Generating the Resolve that is Never Exhausted; and there is the Samādhi of Beholding the Three Realms as Utterly Non-existent.
There is the samādhi of being alone; there is the samādhi of dwelling in one buddha-field and traveling to another buddha-field;
there is the samādhi of causing the Dharma not to be interrupted wherever one may be; there is the samādhi of always encountering the Buddha wherever one may be;
and there is the samādhi of sitting and observing the great armies, great fires, great waters, and great winds of the ten directions without any fear within them.
There is the samādhi of going forth to instruct; there is the samādhi wherein wherever one dwells, one takes only the Dharma as a vessel;
and there is the samādhi wherein good sons and good daughters, upon hearing this samādhi, immediately attain the thought of coming and going without returning.
Such samādhis are inexhaustible; I have now merely described them briefly for the sake of this assembly.

There is the samādhi called "Existence and Non-existence," the samādhi called "Abiding in All Dharmas," the samādhi called "Naming All Wisdoms," the samādhi called "Teaching the Dharma," the samādhi called "Destroying Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas," the samādhi called "Dharma Jewel," the samādhi called "Dhāraṇī of the Nameless Dharma," and the samādhi called "Knowing the Minds of Others."
There is the samādhi of severing all afflictions; there is the samādhi of subduing power and sensual desires; there is the samādhi of extinguishing the various powers of the ten directions;
there is the samādhi of the abiding place of the radiance of wisdom; there is the samādhi of the incalculable;
there is the samādhi of seeing all phenomena as like reflections in water; and there is the samādhi of inexhaustible pure wisdom.
There is the samādhi of emptiness regarding all evils; there is the samādhi of the perception of wishlessness; there is the samādhi of abiding in dhyāna up to nirvāṇa;
there is the samādhi of being like a vajra, free from defilement; there is the samādhi of extreme luminosity;
there is the samādhi of having transcended all afflictions and brought them to an end; there is the samādhi of the vast water-element; and there is the samādhi of adornment.
There is the Samādhi of Adorning the Great Ship; there is the Samādhi of Entering the Nameless; there is the Samādhi of Inexhaustible Joyful Intention;
there is the Samādhi of Dhāraṇī Without Forgetting; there is the Samādhi of Causing All That Is Dark to Be Illuminated;
there is the Samādhi of Making All That One Delights In Become Joyful; there is the Samādhi of Compassionate Conduct; and there is the Samādhi of Purifying Great Pity.
There is the samādhi of entering the equal mind; there is the samādhi of emerging from the equal mind; there is the samādhi known as "already liberated yet not yet liberated";
there is the samādhi of the place from which light comes; there is the samādhi of awakening where there is nothing to awaken to;
there is the samādhi of liberation through wisdom and liberation through instruction; there is the samādhi of manifesting as a lotus flower; and there is the samādhi of detachment from non-existence.
There is the Samādhi of Constant [Recollection]; the Samādhi of Honored Wisdom Without Master; the Samādhi of Valiant Courage That Subdues All;
the Samādhi of Opening and Expanding All Buddha-fields; the Samādhi of Purity and Formlessness; the Samādhi of the Nameless Jewel;
the Samādhi of Being Like the Ocean That Accepts All; and the Samādhi of Vast Supernatural Power.
The Great Samādhi, such as the Samādhi that reaches everywhere in the time it takes to snap one's fingers.
The Bodhisattva Dharmā addressed Śāriputra, saying:
“Because of abiding in wisdom, what you have asked is called ‘inexhaustible. This is the timely hearing of what is heard according to one’s wish.”
Not being conceited about what one has accomplished, never forgetting what has been done, always maintaining a respectful mind as one practices wisdom according to the teachings,
having a mind that receives nothing so as not to lose propriety, never forgetting or confusing the dharmas one performs,
and with a mind like a precious jewel that eliminates all aging and sickness— taking the mind as a vessel for the Dharma; this is called delighting in patience and reflecting upon it.
One should simply contemplate these words with earnestness: delighting only in the Dharma, the mind, and wisdom; being content and having no attachment to what is given at the proper time;
bestowing gifts without partiality toward friend or foe; contemplating with an earnest mind whatever one hears; rejoicing without grasping at anything;
when the mind is thus gladdened, the body becomes light; the mind no longer dwells on external paths, but desires only to hear the flavor of the Dharma.

Regarding the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, they merely wish to hear about *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), merely wish to hear about the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), and wish to hear the bottomless Dharma.
Their intentions are such that their thoughts do not diverge; they desire to receive *upāyakauśalya* with their intent, and they wish to hear the Dharma of non-arising (*anutpāda-dharma*).
They do not crave contemplation, but merely wish to receive the deliverance of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) with their intent.
Desiring to know the sound of impermanence, desiring to know the meaning of tranquility, desiring to know that emptiness is itself empty,
and desiring to know non-conceptuality, birth-and-death, and giving— desiring none of these,
he wishes only to hear music; following the music, he practices faithfulness throughout the ten directions and rightly subdues the faculties of desire.
The Bodhisattva Dharmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“When a bodhisattva has attained the Treasure Tathāgata Samādhi, acting with mastery and having perfected all wisdom, they then obtain the Three Jewels:

first, it is like a reflection in water; the reflection is neither within the water nor outside the water. When the bodhisattva sits here, their body is entirely present throughout the ten directions, yet that body is also not in the ten directions.”

Second, while the Bodhisattva sits here, his manifested bodies appear before the Buddhas of the ten directions and sit there; yet his body does not actually reside before the Buddhas of the ten directions.

Third, it is like the sound of an echo in the mountains that returns as a response; the sound is neither inside nor outside. In the same way, while the Bodhisattva sits here, he can speak of the affairs of all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions from afar; yet none of those Bodhisattvas of the ten directions have come here, nor has he gone to them—it is just so.
The Buddha said to the Bodhisattva Dharmā:

"Having attained the gateway of dhāraṇī, it is like holding a crossbow with arrows ready; wherever one wishes to shoot, there is nowhere it cannot reach. In the same way, when a bodhisattva holds onto a single wisdom and enters into ten trillion wisdoms, there is nowhere it does not reach."
The Buddha told the Bodhisattva Dharmā:

"When you see the Asuras intending to raise their armies, in the mere twinkling of an eye their forces reach the six heavens without any intervening space; it is just so when a Bodhisattva, from the ninth stage downward, intends to preach the Dharma."
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama said to Śāriputra:

"Purity means that greed and desire have been extinguished and subdued; that mind which is free from greed and desire is inexhaustible. As for those various evil intentions that cannot be subdued, they further disturb the mind and protect those evil intentions; therefore, they are inexhaustible."

If the mind is characterized by anger, physical desire for arrogance, or seeks to do what is improper, the Bodhisattva constantly wishes to protect this mind; knowing that it cannot be completely eliminated, one should know that the mind is inexhaustible. One who protects it must not allow it to become indolent, and should thus know that the mind is inexhaustible.
Those who are deranged and chaotic, he protects them by means of the Dharma;

one should know that this intention is inexhaustible. Those without wisdom he desires to protect; knowing that their intentions are inexhaustible, he bestows the Dharma upon all and liberates them through the Dharma; one should know that this intention is inexhaustible. Desiring to instruct all people so that they may all cultivate merit, one should know that this intention is inexhaustible.
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama said to Śāriputra: “A bodhisattva has four dharmas:

first, the practice of mental *dhāraṇī* is inexhaustible; second, the practice of entering into *dhāraṇī* is inexhaustible; third, teaching all beings through *dhāraṇī* is inexhaustible; fourth, because of extensive learning and inquiry, *dhāraṇī* is inexhaustible. These are the four.”
Furthermore, there are four things that are inexhaustible:

first, the higher liberation and the middle liberation are inexhaustible; second, the path of the four horses is boundless; third, the king who accords with the will is boundless; fourth, the twelve links of dependent origination have no master and are inexhaustible. These are the four.

Furthermore, there are nine things that are inexhaustible: first, the discourse on non-self is inexhaustible; second, the perception of non-action is inexhaustible; third, the discourse on the tranquility of nirvāṇa is inexhaustible; fourth, those who are delivered are inexhaustible; fifth, the great ocean and its flowing waters never weary or grow tired are inexhaustible; sixth, all evils and their absence of defilement are inexhaustible; seventh, the sounds of suffering and pain are inexhaustible; eighth, the perceptions of coming and going are inexhaustible; ninth, those who are delivered have no master and are thus inexhaustible. These are the nine.
Furthermore, there are nine things that are inexhaustible: first, the Buddha-fields are inexhaustible;

second, the places from which Bodhisattvas come are inexhaustible; third, those who resolve their minds toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* are inexhaustible; fourth, those who lose their vows and take up the path of Arhats or Pratyekabuddhas are inexhaustible; fifth, Bodhisattvas of the ten directions flying from one Buddha-field to another Buddha-field are inexhaustible; sixth, the six *pāramitās* are inexhaustible; seventh, the three *samādhis* are inexhaustible; eighth, passing beyond *nirvāṇa* as being like an illusion is inexhaustible; ninth, *samādhi* itself is inexhaustible. These are the nine.
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama said to Śāriputra:
"A bodhisattva possesses thirty-two jewels:
the first is that his mind does not cling to sensual desire; this is the inexhaustible perfection of patience."
Second, not giving rise to the notions of self or non-self, nor having anything created; therefore, this forbearance is inexhaustible.
Third, not dwelling upon any good or evil; this is why this forbearance is inexhaustible.
Fourth, harboring no resentment in one's mind toward anything; this is why this forbearance is inexhaustible.
Fifth, not to harbor anger toward any person—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
sixth, not to dwell upon the evils of others—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
seventh, likewise not to falsely harass or strike others—this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Eighth, not engaging in frivolous play within the assembly during a great gathering—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
ninth, protecting oneself and protecting the bodies of others—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
tenth, providing for and protecting those who are poor without expecting anything in return hereafter—this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Eleventh, to exercise self-restraint and not follow evil associates; this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Twelfth, to have no thoughts of craving or desire regarding one's own body or the bodies of others; this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Thirteenth, to give rise to no conceptualizations and to be free from thoughts of good or evil for even as long as a finger-snap; this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Fourteenth, protecting the physical marks adorned with merit—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
fifteenth, believing in the performance of good and not departing from samādhi—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
sixteenth, constantly guarding one's speech and refraining from false words—this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Seventeenth, the purity of mind and intention—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
eighteenth, steadfastly abiding with spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) throughout successive lifetimes, never speaking of their faults or evils to others—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
nineteenth, reflecting for oneself that if another has evil, one likewise possesses evil—this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Twentieth: when thoughts are free from perversity and one immediately awakens to such perversity, this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
twenty-first: having a gentle heart and a harmonious mind, this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
twenty-second: protecting against evil people so that [afflictions] do not arise in the mind, this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Twenty-third: Being born in the heavens to instruct the devas; this is the inexhaustibility of patience. Twenty-fourth:
Being born in the heavenly worlds to teach that one should follow two paths and not revert to three; this is the inexhaustibility of patience. Twenty-fifth:
Being fully endowed with all the various marks of excellence; this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Twenty-sixth: attaining a voice like that of Brahmā; this is the inexhaustibility of patience. Twenty-seventh:
being liberated from lust, anger, and delusion; this is the inexhaustibility of patience. Twenty-eighth:
having no conceptualization regarding forms or names; this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Twenty-ninth: not being attached to the merits one has performed, desiring only to give rise to all dharmas—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
thirtieth: subduing all non-Buddhists—this is the inexhaustibility of patience;
thirty-first: having emerged from all illnesses—this is the inexhaustibility of patience.
Thirty-second: being fully endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas so as not to cause injury or error;
this is the thirty-second inexhaustible treasure.
"Furthermore, Śāriputra!
Furthermore, there are thirty-three matters that constitute the jewels of entry:
first, wishing to enter resonance and wishing to enter contemplation, yet contemplating that there is nothing to contemplate—this is the jewel;
second, wishing to enter the mind while being detached from the mind—this is the jewel.
Third, that the mind has no master is itself the treasure;
fourth, that one wishes to enter the body to seek liberation, yet fundamentally there is no one to be liberated, is itself the treasure;
fifth, that one wishes to enter the twelve links of dependent origination where there is no abiding, is itself the treasure.
Sixth, wishing to enter non-interruption while remaining detached from non-interruption—this is itself a treasure;
seventh, wishing to enter impermanence while viewing it as formless—this is itself a treasure;
eighth, wishing to enter namelessness while remaining detached from namelessness—this is itself a treasure.
Ninth, wishing to enter quiescence without departing from arising—this is a treasure;
tenth, wishing to enter the triple world without departing from the triple world—this is a treasure;
eleventh, receiving that which is not received—this is a treasure.
Twelfth, wishing to enter the future and emerge from the past, as well as the future and the past—this is itself a treasure;
thirteenth, wishing to enter the contemplation of merit and seeing that it fundamentally has no master—this is itself a treasure;
fourteenth, wishing to enter emptiness and [realizing] emptiness within emptiness—this is itself a treasure.
Fifteenth, wishing to enter the signless without giving rise to the notion of the signless—this is itself a treasure;
sixteenth, wishing to enter the wishless while remaining free from wishing—this is itself a treasure;
seventeenth, wishing to enter emptiness while remaining free from the perception of emptiness—this is itself a treasure.
Eighteenth: Entering samādhi without any conjunction; why is this so? Because dharmas are non-dual, this is itself the jewel. Nineteenth:
Not having any aspiration for a place of rebirth by means of samādhi; this is itself the jewel. Twentieth:
Samādhi does not act as a realization for any dharmas; this is itself the jewel.
Twenty-first: To desire to enter the path of non-arising where there is no one to cross over is itself a treasure;
twenty-second: to desire to enter the place of non-arising is itself a treasure;
twenty-third: to desire to enter the place of immovability is itself a treasure.
Twenty-fourth, wishing to enter into the non-self of all things without ever departing from non-self—this is a treasure;
twenty-fifth, wishing to be with birth and death from the very beginning without mutual acquaintance—this is a treasure;
twenty-sixth, wishing to be with samādhi from the very beginning without mutual recognition—this is a treasure.
Twenty-seventh: wishing to enter the sign while having no prior cognition of it—this is itself a treasure;
twenty-eighth: wishing to enter, being able to wish, and having the intention to wish—this is itself a treasure;
twenty-ninth: wishing to enter without recollecting and without having any recollection—this is itself a treasure.
Thirty: To wish to enter the gates of *dhāraṇī* such that there is nothing not encompassed—this is itself a treasure.
Thirty-one: For one who wishes to enter, the desire to commit evil and the non-committing of evil—this is itself a treasure.
Thirty-two: To wish to enter through *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and to make the mind a vessel for the Dharma—this is itself a treasure.
"Thirty-third, wishing to be in accord with all things and not to be distant from them;
this is the thirty-third jewel-like quality.
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:
"Just as one who wishes to enter a city must do so through its gates; if one wishes to know the causes and conditions of non-contention, it is not like self-guarding when wishing to know contention;
if one wishes to know how to avoid speech, it is not like remaining within it;
if one does not wish to move, one must not turn about; if one wishes to be without longing, one must have no conceptualizations."
Those who desire form and color should dwell in right mindfulness; those who do not desire anything else should remain tranquil and self-guarded.
One who is able to guard themselves does not engage in idle talk; because such a person is already complete, they neither exalt themselves nor disparage others.
Those who desire what is expedient will find that their actions do not fail; the attainment of the Way is likewise free from doubt. There is none.
The doubter knows that all is fundamentally non-existent; because one who knows fundamental non-existence has nothing to lose, the three periods of time are equal and without distinction.
Since there is no increase or decrease across the three periods of time, one does not dwell in form (*rūpa*). Not dwelling in form is precisely not dwelling in any phenomena (*dharma*).
When the eye sees form, it is merely the visual faculty that dwells upon it, not the form itself. The same applies to the ear hearing sound.
Each sound has no place of abiding; the nose-consciousness and its fragrances likewise have no place of abiding; the tongue-consciousness and its flavors likewise have no place of abiding.
The mind does not know consciousness, nor does consciousness know the mind; the mind has no place of abiding, just as in fundamental practice there is no conceptualization.

The practice of wisdom regarding each truth is thus: there is no "I" or "mine. In the perception of all phenomena, one perceives only non-self. Wisdom does not know that which exists, nor does that which exists know wisdom; wisdom does not know conditioning, nor does conditioning know wisdom. The Bodhisattva’s mind is never separate from the mind.
The Bodhisattva Dharmā addressed the Buddha, saying:
“If the Path does not unite with conceptualization, is there then something that unites?
The Buddha said:

"All dharmas are not realized through conceptualization; they are taken as dharmas only by means of sound. For example, when a person blows a flute, the sound is mournful and pleasant; it blends with song, and the tones harmonize together. It is thus with all *samādhis*, thus with all transformations (*nirmāṇa*), thus with mindfulness (*smṛti*), and thus with awakening (*bodhi*). Birth and death are nameless and detached from namelessness; mindfulness, transformation, and awakening are likewise. All names have no locus, yet I do not conceptualize them. The conceptualization of non-action is detachment from both detachment and non-detachment. The act of non-action is taken as the conceptualization of action. When conceptualization and formations are tranquil, there is absolutely nothing existing; all dharmas are free from desire, and everything is thus."
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama addressed the Buddha, saying:
"All those who have attained tranquility and do not give rise to desire, having resolved their great doubts, each return to their original place?
The Buddha said:
"All dharmas have no locus; transformations also have no locus; even mindfulness has no locus.
He asked again:
"In the place where birth arises, does a locus of birth exist?"
Is there transformation within the place of transformation, or is there no transformation?
Is there moment-to-moment thought within the place of thought, or is there no thought?
Is there awakening within the place of awakening, or is there no awakening?
The Buddha said:

“To say that birth after birth gives rise to further birth, and that Nirvāṇa is born, is to accord with the intention of the Tathāgata; to say that birth after birth does not give rise to further birth, and that Nirvāṇa is born, is not to accord with the intention of the Tathāgata.

To say that transformation after transformation gives rise to further transformation, and that Nirvāṇa is transformed, is to accord with the intention of the Tathāgata; to say that transformation after transformation does not give rise to further transformation, and that Nirvāṇa is transformed, is not to accord with the intention of the Tathāgata.”

To mind after mind further mind the thought of *nirvāṇa* is to accord with the intention of the Tathāgata; to mind after mind further mind the non-thought of *nirvāṇa* is not to accord with the intention of the Tathāgata.

To awaken after awakening further awaken the awakening to *nirvāṇa* is to accord with the intention of the Tathāgata; to awaken after awakening further awaken the non-awakening to *nirvāṇa* is not to accord with the intention of the Tathāgata.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva spoke in verse:
"All phenomena are without arising; When combined, they are but a single purity.
That which has already arisen does not arise again; Nirvāṇa is likewise in all such cases."
That which is transformed is fundamentally non-existent; in transformation upon transformation, there is no one who is liberated.
Transformation is equal to nirvāṇa—tranquil and without location.
The one who recollects is fundamentally without consciousness; the arising of recollection is merely due to emptiness.
Nirvāṇa is equal to mindfulness; the truth of what is contemplated is thus.
Awakening is the practice of equality; that which is awakened to has no destination, and that which is awakened to has no permanence—this is the Tathāgata.
The place of transformation has no location; that which is awakened reaches nowhere.
If transformations have no locus, all phenomena are likewise so.
The place of birth is fundamentally non-existent; non-arising is its true locus.
The place of transformation has no name; all things are samādhi.
In the foundations of mindfulness, mindfulness both exists and does not exist. From emptiness one reaches that state;
it is not that there was originally nothing to be realized—their wisdom is already thus.
Awakening and practice are not separate; awakening does not depart from its place.
Through practice following awakening, one perceives the Truth; apart from awakening, there is no liberation.
The dharmas that arise are unceasing; wherever they abide, it is always thus.
Among the three thousand suns and moons, there is nothing that illuminates more supremely than the Dharma.
The Dharma is not a product of discursive thought; it is that which one should practice by returning to.
Within desire, no defilement arises; it is neither emptiness nor conceptualization.
The Tathāgata’s mind is ever pure, yet he does not abide in the names of dharmas;
that which is liberated is neither eternal nor permanent, for all things remain as they were in their original state.
Fragrance from flowers comes of itself, yet its source has no fixed location.
Utterly pure and without location, all things are exactly thus.
A withered tree sprouts anew after a thousand years; all this arises from the initial resolve.
One beholds a great radiance, such as has never existed before in the world.
The void became music, and light was seen day and night.
At that time, those in the great assembly all resolved their minds upon Bodhisattvahood;
the people were filled with great joy, as they all heard this sutra.
He immediately shook three thousand worlds, yet attained an unmoving body.
Seeing the Dharma as tranquil silence, namelessness is its true response;
how much more so for all that exists in the world—all things are thus.
Purity does not constitute concentration; delusion and wisdom are fundamentally non-existent.
Purity and delusion share the same original source; since wisdom is fundamentally without one who is liberated, there is no arising of samādhi—everything is thus.
When a Bodhisattva dwells on the stages of the Path, they should attend to that from which [the mind] arises:
five things must not be associated with, for they cause one to fall into the three miserable realms.
By remaining far removed from such conduct, one attains Buddhahood and reaches the ten directions.
Having attained the flavor of the Dharma for a hundred days and practicing this samādhi,
they have all come from various lands, flying to where the Buddha dwells.
The devas and the kings all behold the body of the Buddha.
The mind and will are filled with great joy, and the body becomes entirely light.
One should not dwell on perceptions of form; when contemplating the Dharma, there are the Three Honored Ones.
In the Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra, the three thousandfold world-systems do not exist.
When the Tathāgata first resolved upon his aspiration, he vowed never to be apart from the ten directions;
he would always create great gardens of the Dharma, wherein there is no three-thousandfold world system.
This includes all people within the triple world, as well as those in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven above.
The Buddha Sihadhana, whose title is "God among Gods," sent forth his mind to reach that land, yet returned again in an instant;
the Bodhisattva Matina flew back to the Bamboo Grove.
Śāriputra addressed the Bodhisattva Ratnākara, saying:
"What kind of buddha-field is the land from which you have come? What were your original vows, and how does that infinite land compare?"
Ratnākara replied, "What is the nature of that land of Infinite Excellence? Śāriputra said:
"In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all are bodhisattvas; there are no arhats nor any people of mixed origins, and everything that exists there is made of the seven treasures. Ratnākara said:

"Since I first made my vow, what I have accomplished has not reached such a level as this. I do not wish for anything belonging to the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Since dharmas have no place of arising, how could there be any conceptual thought?"
"In all lands, there are those who give rise to vows; now you have further attained the perception of infinite aspirations.
Śāriputra said, "When you came, you brought with you exquisite flowers. Is it not also an aspiration to value such rare and precious things?"
He replied: "These flowers have no form; they serve merely as a primary condition, and it was within the Bamboo Grove that I transmitted the Dharma to them.
Furthermore, Śāriputra!..."
When one sees a Buddha image and pays it homage, one might ask: "Does the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha truly reside within the image?

Although it does not reside within the image, it is likewise not separate from the image. Those who harbor conceptual thoughts claim there is such majestic spiritual power, yet when one observes with clear discernment, nothing at all is found.

Venerable One, it is like the flower named *kūṭāgāra* in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, which all the devas cherish and delight in; likewise, the Bodhisattva takes the Dharma as the guiding eye for all beings, for that which constitutes the foundation of the Path is simply the mind serving as the vessel for the Dharma.
Śāriputra said: "Does the mind alone have a master? Ratnākara replied:
"The mind unites with all phenomena, and all phenomena unite with the mind; yet the Way has no master, for it takes non-arising as its master. Therefore, it is the vessel of the Dharma."
He further asked Śāriputra:
"Have you seen the transformation yet? He replied:
"I have seen it.
Baolai said, "Where does the Way of Transformation reside?"
"From where do they come, and to where do they go? Śāriputra replied,
"An emanation has no location."
Ratnākara asked, "How do you know it is a transformation? Śāriputra replied:
"Because one sees only that which is manifested and does not see its beginning or end, it is called a 'transformation' (nirmāṇa).
Ratnapāla said: "Therefore, there is nothing that exists."
Śāriputra said: “One who sees has arrived; yet seeing is seeing nothing. What, then, is seeing?
Ratnākara replied:

"To see that all perceptions are like transformations is true vision; to see that unarisen phenomena are like transformations, and that future phenomena are nameless, is true vision; to see that there are no created phenomena and no uncreated phenomena is true vision; to see that there is no creator or transformer, but only the formation of nameless perceptions, is true vision; and to see that the Tathāgata performs the act of non-creation is true vision."
Śāriputra asked: "In this seeing, is there coming and going? Ratnākara replied:
"One who has no coming or going is therefore said to see; if there were coming or going, that would not be seeing—it would be a perverted view.
Śāriputra asked Ratnākara, "Is there anyone who has severed the gateway of the cycle of rebirth?"

Ratnāgama said: "Sarvajñā (all-knowledge) has already seen the gate of formlessness; this is the gate that has already severed the cycle of rebirth. That which is empty can lead to liberation, and that which is without liberation can lead to emptiness. It is like space, which there is nowhere it does not enter."
Why is this? Because there is no place where it functions; therefore, there is nowhere it does not enter. Since its function is detached from the source, its wheel does not turn.
The Bodhisattva Dharmā addressed Ratnāgata, saying:
"I wish to cause all those who are newly learned to attain this Dharma.
Ratnākara said: "Those who wish to attain the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*) should practice nine dharmas:"
First, one should resolve that all people throughout the ten directions shall become bodhisattvas;
second, seeing those with evil intentions, one causes such thoughts not to arise in one's own mind—this is concentration;
third, observing the diligent suffering of the five realms of existence, one desires to liberate them all—this is concentration.
Fourth, not giving rise to the notion of "self" amidst the path of delusion is concentration;
fifth, regarding all that is obscure and desiring to make it clear is concentration;
sixth, ensuring that all meritorious deeds performed are never lost is concentration.
Seventh, viewing all people in the ten directions as equal is concentration;
eighth, observing that one should no longer form perceptions regarding pleasant beings of the past or future is concentration;
ninth, causing all beings in the Buddha-fields to set their minds upon the bodhisattva path without wavering, thereby swiftly attaining samādhi, is concentration.
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Among those currently assembled here, who would not resolve to attain Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi?
The Buddha said to Maitreya:

"In the past, during the time of the Buddha Lohita of the Sandalwood River, I first resolved my mind [for enlightenment]. However, being covered by defilements, I did not attain great wisdom. I merely heard it said that a bodhisattva who resolves his mind shall attain their proper place; yet, dwelling only on emptiness, I failed to find a good teacher, lacked *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means), and remained far removed from spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). Deceived by the King of Desire, my attachments were unceasing, and I lost the *pāramitās*. After sinking for sixty-two *kalpas*, I met with the Buddha Dharmasvabhāva, who severed all my doubts for me. I attained *mūlapratiṣṭhāna* (the fundamental non-existence), established myself within emptiness, and my faculties were immediately severed. Seeing the gate of wisdom, I attained the form of the immovable. From this point onward, as I proceeded further, I turned the wheel of Dharma and received this *samādhi* from the Perfectly Awakened One."

Although he had set his mind [on enlightenment] for sixty-two kalpas, it brought no benefit regarding the Dharma; later, when he met the Buddha Dharmasvabhāva, he obtained the Great Tree, whereupon he again set his mind [on enlightenment]. At the moment he set his mind, ninety billion people together resolved their hearts to seek Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"How many dharmas does one who has first resolved their mind possess?
The Buddha said:
“There are nine dharmas:
first, to remain far removed from assemblies and always set one’s mind on tranquility;
second, to obtain virtuous friends and receive the Dharma from them without loss.”
Third, one should distance oneself from evil associates and not engage in their affairs.

Fourth, one should always remain far removed from five things: first, wicked śramaṇas; second, wicked brāhmaṇas; third, wicked eunuchs; fourth, wicked oxen and horses; and fifth, snakes, scorpions, and venomous insects. One should not associate with these five, for while one has not yet attained the Way, they cause a person to enter hell; therefore, one must keep them at a distance.

Fifth, those who have newly resolved to seek the mind of an arhat or a pratyekabuddha should distance themselves from such people; they should recognize the works of Māra and not engage in affairs with them.
Sixth, one sees the Buddha preaching the profound Dharma only within a dream;

seventh, one resolves the mind solely for the sake of the Dharma, not for food or drink; eighth, one should not frequently assemble with others out of expectation for gain; ninth, one should maintain an impartial mind toward the ten directions and an impartial mind in samādhi, aspiring to sit upon the Buddha’s seat without fear—these are the nine dharmas.
When the Buddha spoke these words, sixty thousand devaputras of desire-realm attained this samādhi. All the devas, flying in mid-air, exclaimed:
"Excellent, excellent!"
"To hear this Dharma brings immeasurable merit.
Maitreya Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying,
"When these devaputras hear this Dharma, do they themselves uphold its merit?"
"Is this through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha?

The Buddha said, "These sons of heaven who have now heard this have in their past lives already served twenty thousand Buddhas and made offerings to their śarīras as vast as Mount Sumeru; yet, despite having such merit, it does not benefit them toward Nirvāṇa."
Now, hearing of this samādhi causes one to destroy the prior merit. Why is this?
All merit planted in previous lives is subject to arising and ceasing; yet this present samādhi destroys existence through emptiness.
Maitreya spoke again:
"Will those who hear this samādhi, hereafter, no longer undergo destruction?
The Buddha said:
"This samādhi can never be destroyed. Why is this?

Because this samādhi has no place of names, no place of perceptions, no place of thoughts, no place of forms, no place of consciousness, no place of majestic power, and no place of conditioned activity seeking liberation."

The purity of samādhi is such that this does not reach that, nor does that reach this; it is free from the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, free from volitional construction, and within transformation, it has no locus of form. It is without the severance of birth and death, nor a locus of non-severance; there is only name, only resonance, and only the locus where wisdom opens. Wisdom reaches nowhere; it is not a vessel of action. Therefore, it cannot be destroyed, it cannot be extinguished, and it is a realm without form. Within desire, it is a realm of non-action and consciousness; it is a realm without the arising of formations, one that does not receive the various flavors of sensation, and is without form. It is without exiting or entering, without a place of birth, and without a place of response. It is tranquil and motionless, without boundaries, and indestructible. To wish to destroy it is the root of great delusion and the gateway to birth and death.
Furthermore, Śāriputra, there are five things that are not upright, with which one should not engage:

first, one should not dwell in duality regarding the Dharma; second, one should not give rise to conceptualizations within the Dharma; third, one should not manifest the right or wrong of various dharmas, for there is no such thing as a name; fourth, one should not have views regarding the future or the past; fifth, all dharmas are indestructible. These are the five.
When a bodhisattva attains this dharma of neither going nor coming, they will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
*The Sutra of the Samādhi of the Ultimate Jewel*, Fascicle Upper.
