Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Dharmarakṣa of the Yuezhi during the Western Jin Dynasty.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying: "If there is one who conceives of suffering and pleasure, they do not depart from suffering and pleasure; this constitutes two dharmas."

A bodhisattva does not depart midway, nor does he depart from above; he is not liberated through separation, nor is there anything to be separated from in the middle. Regarding what is done, he is distant from non-action; this is because that which is produced is like an illusion. By means of illusion one is liberated from illusion; within illusion there is no illusion, and within illusion there are no names. Thus, one does not attain liberation by means of dharmas, nor does one attain liberation apart from dharmas. Within liberation, there is further liberation; this is to be without a master, existing as nothing more than a name.
"To have no knowledge of names within syllables is what constitutes the cessation of the Wheel of Dharma.
Śāriputra said, "The Wheel of Dharma is fundamentally pure and non-existent; who is there to cease the wheel?"
Ratnākara said:
"Not knowing the location of the wheel is itself cessation.
The Buddha said:
"Craving for what is desirable is the root of birth and death; the cessation of phenomena is likewise the non-formation of fetters.
This non-formation is the non-departure from formation. To depart from craving for all that is desirable is to be without interruption.
When there is no craving, there is no arising; this is the Path. There is neither the acceptable nor the unacceptable, neither arising nor non-arising."
Neither consciousness nor non-consciousness; neither death nor non-death; neither cessation nor non-cessation; neither distance nor non-distance.

In all that is acceptable or unacceptable, there is dwelling in non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*); yet, being free from non-conceptualization, there is no thought and no recollection. What is taught is nothing taught;
*nirvāṇa* is without extinction, yet it is free from the non-extinction of *nirvāṇa*; it is formless, yet it is free from formlessness.
Nirvāṇa is called the extinction where nothing remains to be extinguished; all phenomena are quiescent and yet detached from quiescence.
All phenomena are neither acceptable nor unacceptable, and there is nothing lost. Within wisdom, one is detached from the root; it is nameless and beyond conceptualization.
That which is illuminated has nothing to be illuminated; within light and darkness, there is no knower of signs. Where delusion and wisdom have no mutual entry, therein—
The Way has no one who attains it; whether in suffering or joy, there is no mutual recognition. What arises is free from the perception of objects;
in purity, there is neither difficulty nor ease. That which delivers has no master; that which is reached has no separation.
All dharmas are not names, yet they are detached from non-names. That which delivers is like flowing water; in names, there is none.
As for "transformation," such things as these are all the Way itself.

The Buddha uses samādhi to deliver beings according to their inclinations, adorning himself with all phenomena; yet this adornment is formless, it is an adornment of inverted views, it is the adornment of the various kings of agreeable objects—it is merely the adornment of perception and non-perception.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Among these devas and humans who have come to this assembly, how many have attained this samādhi?"
The Buddha said to Mañjuśrī:

“All those present in this assembly—gods and humans alike—have universally attained this samādhi and reached these merits; they shall all become buddhas and receive the prediction of their exalted destiny, bringing an end to the five realms of existence.”

At that time, having heard what the Buddha spoke, eight thousand *koṭis* of devas and humans all attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). They immediately ascended into the air to a height of three hundred *zhang* above the ground; on each of their bodies were ten billion flowers and incense, and then they descended to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.

The Bodhisattva Aru and the Bodhisattva Hādi rose from their seats and addressed the Buddha, saying, "These superior men are flying in mid-air; from where do the flowers and incense upon their bodies originate?"
The Buddha said:
"It is like pure white silk that is inherently clean and bright; whatever five colors it is dyed with will appear fresh and beautiful.
The silk is inherently pure, and the colors are inherently pure; through the causal conditions of these two things, they become bright and excellent."
Form does not enter into the cloth, nor does the cloth enter into form; it is through pure causes and conditions that they manifest clarity.
Because the Bodhisattva is pure, he brings forth flowers and incense; the causes and conditions for this are likewise so.

The Bodhisattva does not abide within the flowers and incense, nor do the flowers and incense adhere to the Bodhisattva. When gods and humans sever their conceptual thoughts and attain the dharma of clear wisdom, they then perceive flowers; because the flowers are pure, they arise through causes and conditions. The dharma is likewise so.

Those who dwell in non-abiding accomplish all merits, whereas those who practice while dwelling in conceptualizations open the gates of birth and death. The reason why Arhats and Pratyekabuddhas remain far removed from the five realms of existence is solely due to their ten inverted views:
first, to view all meritorious qualities as being entirely mere verbal expressions is an inverted view;
second, to view the hardships of the five realms and desire to attain Nirvana is an inverted view.
Third, to perceive that all phenomena are impermanent and thus desire to quickly distance oneself from them is an inverted view;
fourth, to seek a state of security when there is originally no such basis is an inverted view;
fifth, to know that there is no exit from the world and no place of entry, yet to fail to cease seeking an exit because the world itself lacks one, is an inverted view.

Sixth, when an Arhat attains Nirvana, fire spontaneously issues from within his body, yet that fire has no external source; if he then gives rise to the thought that the fire from within his body is burning him, he thereby knows that birth and death are not severed—this is a perverted view.
Seventh, while the beginning and end are inexhaustible, he seeks their exhaustion for himself—this is a perverted view.
Eighth, desiring to extinguish all evils in Nirvana, he fails to realize there is no master [to be extinguished] and instead wishes to extinguish it—this is a perverted view.
Ninth, when giving, one does not inspire the minds of others, but desires only that the Dharma not be interrupted; this is a perverted view.
Tenth, regarding suffering and pleasure, one does not practice with equal purity but claims there are two distinct dharmas; this is a perverted view.
"When practicing the bodhisattva path, you should know these matters and quickly distance yourselves from them.
The Buddha spoke to the Bodhisattvas Aruṇa, Mati, and others:

"The various devas and those present in this assembly were all followers of the Buddha Akṣobhya in a former age. That they are now all receiving their predictions before me is because, in past lives, they had already received this samādhi under sixty thousand Buddhas; it is for this reason that they receive their predictions here today."

In the future, when my Dharma is on the verge of being severed, there shall be four hundred thousand people who will uphold the Dharma and cause it to endure without interruption. After that long period, there will be wicked śramaṇas or those who violate the precepts, who shall destroy my Dharma.
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying,
“In what way does a bodhisattva protect the Dharma so that it is not interrupted?
The Buddha said to Subhūti:

"These four hundred thousand bodhisattvas have all attained the eighth stage and below; regarding the Dharma, they harbor thoughts of weariness and burden, yet this serves to protect and uphold the Dharma so that it shall not be severed."
Subhūti addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What constitutes one who destroys the Dharma?
I pray that the Buddha will explain this.”
The Buddha told Subhūti:

“If there are those who have attained the state of an Arhat or a Pratyekabuddha, or even śramaṇas, devas, and humans, who give rise to conceptualizations and harbor burdensome attachments toward the Dharma in pursuit of fame; who destroy and disorder their fundamental wisdom by arbitrarily adding to or subtracting from the Dharma; who provide peripheral and derivative explanations, using the false to mislead the true and using sophistry to confuse the Way; who do not contemplate the wisdom of emptiness but instead strive for outward ornamentation; who hear that Buddhahood can be attained and set their minds on surpassing others in its acquisition; who do not understand *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) and do not diligently cultivate virtuous conduct—these are thieves of the Dharma, destroyers of my Way.”
The Āśvī devas, the Panatī devas, the Tilunī devas, the Kuśudī devas, and the Śanarī devas all addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We pray that you maintain your physical life to entrust it to those who uphold the Dharma; for billions of kalpas, without ceasing, may you always cause us to attain this samādhi."
The Buddha said: "If there are virtuous people who practice this samādhi and do not deviate from the Dharma, they will swiftly attain Buddhahood.

Those who resolve their minds to practice this samādhi are like the precious jewel in the Heaven of No-Thought (Nirvāṇa-deva), the king of all jewels, the most honored among all treasures in heaven and on earth. This jewel appears only when a Buddha is in the world; it is called the *maṇi* jewel of refinement. If one obtains this jewel and places it in a vessel or holds it in the hand, and gazes toward the four directions into the air, one can cause as much rain of precious treasures as desired to fall wherever one turns; nothing fails to accord with one's wishes. One should not be greedy for or begrudge this noble jewel, but should cause it to rain down throughout the triple world so that all may obtain its treasure. The virtue of this samādhi is likewise."
The King of Rājagṛha addressed the Buddha, saying:

“The Buddha is the Honored Protector and the Great Guide of the world; you constantly possess great compassion to rescue and deliver those throughout the ten directions. We pray that you will cause a rain of precious jewels to fall upon our kingdom, so that all the people may universally obtain benefit and merit.”
The Buddha then smiled, and his divine radiance blazed forth.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, stepped forward, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha does not smile without cause; I pray that you will explain its meaning."
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you see this king?

He wishes to obtain the precious jewels of Nirvāṇa from the heavens and rain them down upon Rājagṛha so that it may become universally prosperous. He does not know that he has already attained this treasure through the *Āgata-ratna-samādhi* (the Samādhi of the Coming of Jewels)."
The Buddha said to the king:

"Have you not seen that for a hundred days the people have gone without food, yet they have all attained peace and security, taking the Dharma as their nourishment? Furthermore, all women have been transformed into men—is not the benefit of this Dharma truly great?"

The king’s heart was filled with joy; he immediately removed his precious jewels and scattered them over the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas. These transformed into flower canopies arrayed in the air, amidst which there were hundreds of thousands of musical instruments. The king leaped for joy all the more, forgetting even the thought of eating.
The king addressed the Buddha, saying,
“From where does this flower canopy emerge?
The Buddha replied:
"It emerges from nowhere.
He asked again:
"From what does 'nowhere' emerge?"
The Buddha said:
"It arises from nowhere.
He asked again:
“Since there is nothing that arises, from where does it come?
The Buddha said:
“It comes from the unarisen.”
He asked again:
"From where does that which is unarisen come? He replied:
“I have come from the Immovable.
He asked again,
“From where does the Immovable come?”
He replied, "It has come from non-creation.
He asked again:
“From where does the unconditioned come?
He replied, “It comes from the nameless.”
He asked again:
"From where does 'namelessness' come?
He replied:
"It comes from non-arising.
He asked again,
"From where does non-arising come?"
He replied,
"It comes from the absence of sound.
He asked again:
“From where does this soundless come?
He replied,
“It comes from non-duality.”
He asked again:
"From where does non-duality come?
He replied:
"It comes from formlessness.
He asked again,
"From where does formlessness come?"
He replied, "I have come from the natural state.
He asked again:
"From where does nature come? He replied,
"It comes from transformation."
He asked again:
"From where does this transformation come?
He replied:
“[He] has come apart from transformation.
He asked again:
“Apart from transformation, from where has he come?”
He replied, "It comes from a place where there is mutual knowing apart from non-transformation.
He asked again:
“From where does this state of non-perception arise?
The Buddha said,
“It is for this reason that they are called all dharmas.”
Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the king was filled with even greater joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“These bodhisattvas have come from afar; I pray that you invite them all to come to my palace tomorrow.”
The Buddha immediately granted his consent and accepted their invitation.

The king returned to the palace and prepared the offerings, adorning the roads with canopies, banners, and streamers of brilliant beauty. Within the palace, seats were fashioned entirely from precious jewels; the queen and her attendants observed the fasts and paid their utmost respect.
On the following day, Mañjuśrī, Ratnāgama, and the other bodhisattvas went together to the royal palace.
Bodhisattva Ratnāgama yielded precedence to Mañjuśrī, saying:
"Now, these superior persons should enter first."

The Bodhisattvas said: "In wisdom there is no location; in the mind there is no form; in mindfulness there is no conceptualization; in the Dharma there is nothing to be bestowed, yet what is bestowed does not depart from the Path. Having severed [attachment] regarding the Wheel of Dharma, one has neither thought nor conceptualization toward the Dharma, nor any notions of much or little. One who is thus is therefore honored; having entered extensively into skillful means, they have no cognition of marks regarding omniscience (sarvajñatā). Having donned the armor of the Dharma, they neither increase nor decrease in samādhi. Such a person is therefore honored and should accordingly stand at the front."
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama replied:
"Now these superior persons are advanced in years and eminent in virtue; for this reason they are to be honored and should enter first.
The bodhisattvas said:

"Our years are like withered trees; their roots are already dead, they bear no flowers or leaves, and they provide little shade, being of meager benefit to the world. Although you, O Benevolent One, are young, you have entered into profound wisdom. You are like a jewel tree that greatly benefits the world; for this reason you are the most venerable, and it is fitting that you go first."
Once they had all entered the palace and taken their seats, the devas above delighted them with music.
The king sent his queen and the court ladies to burn various famous incenses and present offerings. When the meal was finished, the king asked Ratnāgama:
"I now wish to see the Buddhas of the ten directions; what dharma should I practice to be able to see them?"
Ratnākara said: “Those who wish to see the Buddhas should practice nine dharmas: first, viewing the Buddhas of the ten directions as no different from these;

second, viewing the Way as having no path; third, viewing all people as none being liberated; fourth, viewing food and drink as like that which is seen in a transformation; fifth, knowing that the five aggregates have no consciousness or perception; sixth, knowing that the six sense faculties are to be viewed as like an illusion; seventh, knowing that what is observed is merely an inverted view; eighth, making great offerings within the Dharma; ninth, knowing that in what is given there is nothing given—these are the nine.”

"Emptying the mind, viewing all things with equanimity, and being without the distinction of self and other; with a tranquil will, attaining pure concentration, and seeing nothing—then one sees the Buddha everywhere.
At that time, he praised Ratnākara, saying:
"How wonderful! How wonderful!"
"It is exactly as you have said.
The Buddha spoke in verse:
"May this kalpa always be so; may those born always encounter the Honored One."
Having received great wisdom, one constantly eradicates the root of craving and desire.
Without greed and without envy, evil intentions no longer arise;
thus, before countless Buddhas, one attains the hearing of this samādhi.
Entering into the three thousandfold world-systems, he constantly practices the honored samādhi;
toward all people, he regards them as no different from all manner of precious jewels.
The Dharma does not arise from the five aggregates, nor does it depart from their location.
From contemplation one attains the name of liberation; all things are thus.
From contemplation one attains joy, giving rise to a mind that is non-arising.
Since its state is already such, he is therefore the God among Gods.
If one is within the three realms, there is neither birth nor death;
as for nirvāṇa and nirvṛti, none of these exist at all.
One’s mind should not harbor wrong thoughts, nor should one perform unrighteous deeds.
If one is within the three realms, one should maintain the mind so that it does not arise.
Though sounds may have their echoes, and the internal and external correspond, when nothing arises, all is utterly tranquil; all phenomena are likewise thus.
The names of the three thousand buddha-fields are all like this;
they are neither heard nor seen, and are not subjects for discussion as phenomena.
This samādhi is beyond calculation; it is held as manifold through the power of number.
The wise who understand these words attain the Buddha’s state of impermanence.
The Dharma is entirely pure, vast and peerless;
it constantly acts as boundless water, carrying and covering the three thousandfold world-system.
The *āśaya-dhāraṇī*: When the resolve is first awakened, there is nothing before it;
since the Dharma is already thus, all should practice it accordingly.
I recall when I sought the Dharma in the past, throughout many kalpas.
With a mind always intent on renouncing the home life, they seek nothing within the realm of desire.
Constantly relying upon virtuous friends, they establish themselves in the abiding of the True Dharma;
at that time, amidst the great assembly, they hear of the Honored Samādhi.
With hearts full of great joy, they immediately stayed in mid-air,
one hundred and forty *zhang* above the ground, with palms joined beside the Buddha.
Those bodhisattvas now seated here receive their predictions in this very same way.
Their minds filled with increasing joy, they hear of all the samādhis;
then, from a single buddha-field, they fly before the various Buddhas,
neither moving nor shaking, yet causing all the lands to tremble.
The Dragon King was greatly delighted and immediately rained down ten thousand kinds of incense,
which transformed into various pools of water reaching up to the middle of the three-thousandfold world system.
Fragrant flowers arrived spontaneously, and turbulent winds arose naturally.
"A hundred kinds of musical instruments all abide in the air.

Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Ratnamati asked Mañjuśrī, "Now these fragrant flowers have come from other lands, and these musical instruments have arrived within this assembly; is this through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha?"
"Is it through the power of a bodhisattva? Mañjuśrī replied:
"The power and spiritual transformations attained by both Buddhas and bodhisattvas are all invisible. To know this joy is to know the joy that is nameless; it exists wherever there is presence."
The sound of the Dharma has no place of name; if one delights in this delight, all that exists is like an illusion—this is joy.
The non-dual Dharma is joy; the desire to deliver all arhats and pratyekabuddhas is joy;
the desire to cause those seen on heterodox paths to all attain Buddhahood is joy; that there is no master over those delivered is joy. All...
To dwell in non-abiding and have nothing that arises is bliss; to be free from the burden of affliction within samādhi is bliss;
for all places to be nameless is bliss; for all that exists to be like an illusion is bliss; for the sphere of non-sound to be a place of non-arising is bliss;
for there to be no giving within the Dharma-gift is bliss; and for there to be no place of permanence within the great trichiliocosm is bliss.
This is bliss: causing all people to attain faith in non-attainment is bliss;
that which is entirely inexhaustible throughout the three periods of future, past, and present is bliss; causing them to return to the original state where nothing is seen is bliss;
seeing the Wheel of Dharma as being without anything seen is bliss; and that all things within the three thousandfold world-system are equal is bliss.
Bliss is the treasury of the Dharma within the three thousandfold worlds of the ten directions; bliss is that in the lands of the ten directions there are only names;
bliss is the union of form and desire; bliss is that names have no master; bliss is the boundless and all-encompassing stillness;
bliss is the union of all light and darkness; and bliss is never losing sight of whatever practices are undertaken.
The precepts are bliss; that all thoughts do not depart from samādhi is bliss; the perfection of the jewel of space is bliss;
that all wisdom-awakenings have no fixed location is bliss; that all things are acceptable is bliss; that there is ultimately no one who receives [karmic results] is bliss;
that there is nothing equal to it within the three realms is bliss; and to be insatiable in craving for the Dharma is bliss.
Cherishing life is joy; all that is clear and further clarified is joy; to abandon all inverted views and see correctly is joy;
practicing generosity without expectation is joy; the mind’s boundless activity as a great captain is joy;
the infinite liberation from the garden of existence is joy; and the tranquility of the mind is joy.
To have no fixed attachment to what is pleasant is bliss; for the various gates of samādhi to be free from inversion is bliss;
to neither hear nor listen is bliss; for all thoughts to be non-conceptual is bliss; that all people are without liberation is bliss;
for all that is saved to be like an illusion is bliss; and for the initial aspiration to be conjoined with samādhi is bliss.
Bliss is that from which all bodhisattvas come; there is no fixed location for this bliss.
Bliss is that when bodhisattvas travel throughout the ten directions by means of their minds; it is not blue, yellow, white, or black, and it is a bliss that has no physical path.
"Thus it is, Ratnāgama!
If you wish to know the joy of the music produced by the majestic spiritual power of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, it is like this.
Then the Bodhisattva Ratnāgama spoke in verse:
“Mañjuśrī’s intention is such that his venerable wisdom has no predecessor;
the wretched three-thousandfold world-system he bestows upon, none of its wisdom fails to revere him.
Through the practice of his majestic spiritual power, he completely eliminates [defilements] within the three-thousandfold world-system.”
Among all pleasures, there is no desire; it is solely for the sake of liberation that one gives.

The joy of the Dharma is the greatest; toward those who have not been transformed and are not yet liberated, one bestows the gift of the joyful Dharma, even as if toward those who are empty and unliberated.
The Dharma proceeds together with bliss; there is no treasure superior to this.
That which is cherished has no owner, like space, it has no fixed location.
Deeply penetrating all that is subtle and wondrous, one understands all people.
Causing them to attain the Great Dharma, he cuts off the roots of diligent suffering.
All people in the world have minds that do not understand;
taking the Dharma as the mind of awakening, he saves all through wisdom.
At that time, the Buddha spoke these verses for the sake of the Bodhisattva Ratnāgama from afar:
"To be apart from emptiness yet not non-conceptual—this conceptualization is not emptiness. To give rise to no thought regarding phenomena is itself the arising."
One should always maintain a gentle mind, pure and devoid of anything possessed; though form and desire appear to unite, there is no one who enters into them.
What is taught is formless, yet it does not depart from that which has form; because phenomena are like dreams, that which is perceived has no bottom.
This is quiescence and the departure from quiescence; there is no departing and no creating. All phenomena have no master;
that which is perceived is like a magical transformation.
There is nothing at all to be received, and no phenomenon to be abandoned. Regarding what is done and what is seen—all is thus.
Not form, yet not separate from form; this form is not apart [from it]. Its dharma is like form, and its locus is thus.
Not sound, yet an echo; neither heard nor seen, neither listened to nor observed—everything is thus.
In transformation there is no name; one speaks of it as "this," yet in the Dharma there is no such reckoning—such is that which is delivered.
In illusion there is no seeing; what is seen is free from seeing. Free from craving for all desires, this is not the conduct of the non-Dharma.
Untainted by desire, neither attached nor detached; seeing thus with truth, there is no seer.
Pure and free from purity, unconditioned throughout the ten directions; whatever exists is as it truly is—like a transformation, without a master.
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama, understanding what the Buddha had said, then spoke these verses within the palace:
"Fundamental doubt is not understood; One claims that all phenomena are thus. Originally there is no permanence;
Doubt and wisdom are like this."
To be weary of perception, to find suffering in consciousness and recollection, and to rely on names and dwell upon words—this is not the seeker of the Dharma.
In the fundamental state it is not thus; there is no returning and no "not-is. That which is acceptable is itself nothing to be accepted; one remains far removed from anything that could be accepted.
Liberation from birth is non-extinction; this itself is extinction. To have no perception of extinction is non-extinction.
Regarding phenomena, there is no arising, nor does one conceive of their formation. Why is this so?
All dharmas are empty.
Nor do they seek to say, "I am apart from nirvāṇa. Why is this?
Because they are pure in their beginning and end.
Not exhausting the ten directions, one raises them up as testimony; if there is speech that says "this is me," this itself constitutes testimony.
One should not dwell on distant thoughts, but rather contemplate the ten directions: dharmas have no dual nature, and thus one immediately attains namelessness.
The Dharma is not a matter of thought; that which can be attained is reached through such practice. One does not perceive a "venerable Dharma" as an object.
It is essential to understand wisdom, to be without fear regarding the sublime, and to practice deeply without grasping—this may be called the gateway to wisdom.
The Bodhisattva Ratnāgama asked Mañjuśrī:
“Among those newly resolved for enlightenment now present in this assembly, I wish to enable them to attain the infinite Dharma; by what means should this be accomplished?”
Mañjuśrī replied, “By having no mental construction regarding perceptions, one immediately attains the ultimate Dharma.
He asked again:
"What is meant by 'the non-performing agent'?
Mañjuśrī replied: "It refers to attaining the nine precious dharmas:"

First, that the mind has no locus is itself the Jewel; second, that observing phenomena (dharma) has no master is itself the Jewel; third, that not perceiving a future or a past is itself the Jewel; fourth, that regarding phenomena there is no creator is itself the Jewel; fifth, that what is given is given only as the Dharma-scriptures is itself the Jewel; sixth, that seeing the suffering of the five realms of existence and not turning away from them is itself the Jewel; seventh, that what is realized is not distant from *upāyakauśalya* (skillful means) is itself the Jewel; eighth, that directly seeing all phenomena and not abiding in duality regarding phenomena is itself the Jewel; ninth, that even reaching *nirvāṇa* is like a transformation is itself the Jewel. These are the nine Dharmas that are Jewels.
Thereupon Mañjuśrī spoke in verse:
"Where there is nothing for which one has desire, And where that which abides is without a fixed name;
If it is empty and free from defilement, Then the Buddha’s smile is not without cause."
Laughing at emptiness does not depart from the phenomenal;
as originally there was no one who laughed, one already dwells within the names of all dharmas, and thus everything is like laughter.
Both the fundamental and the derivative are spontaneous; there is no one who comes or goes.
One who laughs has a response; one who does not respond does not laugh.
All phenomena (dharmas) are one; once there is laughter, there is duality.
In duality there are no names; therefore, he is the Honored One.
In his laughter there is no attachment; he bestows the gift of the Dharma upon all beings.
Though moved, he remains unmoved; therefore, he is the Unsurpassed Honored One.
In his laughter there is no requital; in all things, there is no master.
That smile does not depart from the fundamental; therefore, O God among Gods, the smiler has no arising, for it is merely due to inverted views.
Within all dharmas, there is total quiescence; that which is quiescent is fundamentally non-existent.
The one who laughs does not depart from transformation; through transformation, he bestows great gifts.
Within transformation, there is no name to be raised; therefore, this is the Dharma.
Within the Dharma, there is nothing of this kind; it is merely the gift of non-liberation.
That which is liberated is not liberation; the Buddha is also like this.
Therefore, within the great assembly, he deliberates on the deliverance of those who are not to be delivered; his bestowal of the Dharma has no peer.
Śāriputra asked Ratnākara:
"If one wishes to cause all learners throughout the ten directions to attain the dhāraṇīs of total retention,
what dharma must they practice to achieve this?"
Ratnākara said: "One should practice thirty-two dharmas of the jewel:
first, one should desire to deliver all those who have not yet resolved their minds, delivering them as if by transformation without obstruction."
Second, to cause all those who have not yet resolved their minds toward the unsurpassed, right, and true path to abide in the True Dharma;
third, to regard the three thousand great thousandfold world systems as equal and without distinction;
fourth, to lead those who dwell in limitations away from the various desires so that they may enter the gateway of wisdom, remaining unmoving and unchanging until they reach nirvana.
Fifth, when people say there is a heaven or that there is no heaven, his resolve remains unshaken;
sixth, his resolve for the Way is firm and solid, and his mind is not timid or weak;
seventh, regarding all who come to receive birth, he views the future and the past as being without duality.
Eighth, one contemplates that all samādhis and dhyānas are tranquil and have no fixed location;
ninth, all those who are delivered have no master, for everything proceeds from emptiness to emptiness;
tenth, I receive the Dharma from all the Buddhas throughout the trichiliocosm.
Eleventh, may all those from other buddha-fields who dare to come and listen to this sutra attain definitive resolution;
twelfth, regarding the flowers and incense found in all buddha-fields, may those who come feel no attachment to them, and those who do not come feel no longing for them;
thirteenth, may all who resolve their minds attain the stability of the Dharma.
Fourteenth, their minds regarding the future and the past shall be without increase or decrease; why is this?
Because they know that, fundamentally, there is no duality.
Fifteenth, they desire to cause all sentient beings, from the crawling insects to the flying creatures throughout the ten directions, to uphold the prohibitive precepts and never violate them.
Sixteenth, there are no deviant thoughts regarding the ten directions; turning the mind back to its source, one then proceeds toward the gate of wisdom.
Seventeenth, there is nothing one cannot endure, and one is always free from deviant resentment.
Eighteenth, from one contemplation to the next, there is no one who attains [liberation].
Nineteenth, it is as originally non-abiding and having no place of permanent residence;
twentieth, that which is delivered has no master, being like space, free from thought and conception;
twenty-first, in bestowing wisdom there is no one who raises up a name, and by being unattached to desire, one thereby attains liberation.
Twenty-second: because what is taught does not depart from giving based on causes;
among the multitudes in great kingdoms, there are none who are not liberated.
Twenty-third: flying to other lands across countless realms, one remains unimpeded in the presence of all Buddhas.
Twenty-fourth: viewing all lands as equal, such that none can escape [the truth];
twenty-fifth: purifying ignorance so that it merges with original purity without distinction;
twenty-sixth: dwelling within the great trichiliocosm to act as a bridge, exhorting those who have not yet awakened to see the light where there was darkness.
Twenty-seventh, he acts as a great captain upon the great ocean, ferrying all living beings across without ever becoming weary;
twenty-eighth, he acts as an infinite canopy that shuts out all defilements;
twenty-ninth, he acts as boundless wisdom that never departs from the ten directions.
Thirty: He exercises great compassion to encompass and nourish all beings; because he shall deliver all those who have not yet been delivered, he is titled the God among Gods. Thirty-one:
He constantly practices an impartial mind without partiality, providing peerless salvation and succor; therefore, he is titled the Unsurpassed Honored One and Benefactor. Thirty-two:

What the Bodhisattva speaks does not depart from the sutras and the Dharma; throughout the myriad lands of the great trichiliocosm, there is none who does not hear it equally, and for this reason, flowers naturally arise in the air.
"These are the thirty-two dharma-jewels of a bodhisattva.
Thereupon, the Bodhisattva Ratnāgata spoke in verse:
"The ten directions are everywhere like illusions; All things are impermanent."
The true Dharma is the correct truth of tranquility; expounding it, one delivers sentient beings.
To have perceptions is not to be free from perception; all things are fundamentally empty in reality.
Just as when a flower has not yet put forth its leaves, its color cannot be grasped.
All that is desired by the multitude, he establishes as the King of Pleasure;
the Unsurpassed Honored One among all jewels is titled the God among Gods.
Therefore, within the great assembly, he deliberates upon delivering those who have not yet been liberated.
Its essence is fundamentally without permanence; Thus he is titled the Honored One of Ten Powers.
All things are viewed through inverted perspectives; The world calls this state "darkness.
If one can regard all that exists as like an illusion, One will be able to liberate those within the ten directions.
In the impermanent realm of empty space, the Buddha-treasury is entirely contained within;
because it is liberated yet there is no one to be liberated, he teaches the people of the ten directions.
All the buddha-fields of the ten directions, when joined together, become a single land.
A great assembly of beings naturally gathers, filling all throughout the ten directions.
The Buddha, the All-Awakened One, does not let his smile depart from his countenance,
nor does he abandon his golden hue, as he reveals himself to those who have not yet been liberated.
Acting as guides for the ten directions, their minds never depart from the Dharma King;
though they practice giving, there is nothing given, as flowers are scattered throughout the ten directions. Golden great lotuses fill all of space.
Arising from conceptualization, they engage in practice, yet do not abide among the various devas.
The mind of Mañjuśrī is vast and peerless;
those who have received the prediction of attaining the Way dwell within the midst of empty space.
The Honored One, Jewel-Come Wisdom-Mind, His radiance pervades the entire palace;
All the celestial beings who find delight therein Have fully attained the Dharma-gate.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten directions Are moved throughout all the buddha-fields.
Now that the various devaputras have assembled, having been able to hear this honored sutra,
they clearly perceive all things and arrive at their delightful palaces.
These are transformed into canopies of interlaced jewels, with ten thousand kinds of celestial flowers and incense.
Listening to and receiving the various samādhis, sitting and observing within the great assembly,
those who have come with long-accumulated merit and have resolved their minds to make offerings to the Honored One—
such practitioners do not see [the Buddha] directly; all that exists is likewise thus.
"The various liberations are beyond numbering; the three realms are inexhaustible.
Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva asked Ratnākara:
"All sounds are like transformations, and the dharmas they produce are without conceptualization and likewise inexhaustible; therefore, there is spontaneity (svabhāva)."

"By what means should one be liberated from it? Ratnākara replied: "There are nine treasures of the Dharma: [1] the treasure of faith, [2] the treasure of precepts, [3] the treasure of generosity, [4] the treasure of wisdom, [5] the treasure of diligence, [6] the treasure of patience, [7] the treasure of truth, [8] the treasure of loving-kindness, and [9] the treasure of equanimity."
First, that which is spontaneous has no location and is like an illusion;
second, all phenomena have no location and are like an illusion;
third, that which is yet to come has no location and is like an illusion.
Fourth, all existing worldly realms are also like transformations;
fifth, observing past realms as being like transformations;
sixth, observing and seeing all phenomena as merely like illusions, such that there are no realms at all, which are likewise like transformations.
Seventh, that which is seen has no location and is like a transformation;
eighth, the attainment of the Way has no place of liberation and is like a transformation;
ninth, the attainment of nirvāṇa fundamentally has no place of abiding and is like a transformation.
"These are the nine dharmas by which one may attain the wisdom of liberation.
Mañjuśrī asked again:
"Since even that which transcends nirvāṇa is likewise spontaneous, who is the original source of this transformation?"
Who is the master of transformation?
Is that which is transformed fundamentally non-existent?
Does that which is transformed have a place of origin, or is it non-existent?
"Is the Way something that exists in a place, or does it not? Ratnākara replied:
"There are nine dharmas by which one knows that transformation has no location:"

First, that which is not a path and has no location is transformation; second, that transformation has no location and is without thought is transformation; third, that the transformer has no arising and the place of transformation has no location is transformation; fourth, that which is not a permanent name and has no time of exhaustion is transformation; fifth, that the place of transformation has no location is transformation; sixth, that there is no thought regarding the path is transformation; seventh, that the transformer, regarding arising, has no arising is transformation; eighth, that the transformer, regarding all desires, has no location is transformation; ninth, that the transformer, regarding that which is to be delivered, has no location is transformation. These are the nine dharmas for knowing the root of transformation.
Thereupon Mañjuśrī replied with a verse:
“In the ten directions there is no one who creates emanations; Emanation after emanation has no form.
All things are impermanent treasures; Therefore, he is the Lord of Emanations.”
The Way is not attained through transformation, nor does it depart from its place;
what is taught has no fixed form, for it exists naturally in its own place.
All treasures are attained through transformation; fundamentally, they are detached and non-existent.
His origin is identical with transformation; therefore, he is the Honored One among men.
Desire arises from transformation, yet in the fundamental nature of dharmas, such a thing does not exist.
Through transformation one dwells in the five realms of existence, yet no one perceives a master of transformation.
Birth and death, as well as the five destinies, are not connected to the transformation-body;
yet because worldly craving is not severed, he manifests as Perfectly Awakened.
The Tathāgata and the Lord of Transformations are the supreme and infinite Honored Ones of the ten directions.
He sustains and transforms the world to make it great, yet there is no one in the world who knows him.
The Wheel of Dharma turns without form; in that transformation, there is no one who turns it.
Bound by form, there is conceptual thought; in the profound Dharma, there is no one who turns it.
Manifesting forms throughout the ten directions, there are none who do not receive the Dharma;
the great wisdom thus bestowed is such that no one in the world can describe it.
Neither those with worldly desires nor the Arhats have attained this realization of the Jewel.
Therefore, within the great assembly, he extensively expounds the treasure of non-duality.
His wisdom is inexhaustible, his radiance is supreme and peerless;
acting as a bridge for the ten directions, that which he teaches is without duality.
May all the Buddha-fields of the ten directions be made entirely equal,
and may those people therein never give rise to divergent thoughts.
May the gardens of the dharmas of the ten directions purify all beings from their defilements.
Nor does one come from the world; regarding phenomena, there is no one who is liberated.
There is no liberation within wisdom, nor is there anyone seen coming or going.
Within stillness, one sees stillness again; within clarity, one sees clarity once more.
The Dharma is not attained through wisdom; it is naturally and fundamentally non-existent.
When wisdom and darkness are merged in sameness, there is thus no one who perceives characteristics.
Ignorance and wisdom are not merged; yet that wisdom illuminates the multitude of darknesses.
That which is bestowed is for the sake of the Dharma alone, like flowers upon a high mountain.
All evils cannot be exhausted; sensual desires cannot be ended.
Nirvana and birth-and-death—all things are thus.
"The wisdom of the Buddhas of the ten directions is without knowing and without perceiving;
because they perceive the pure dharma, it is said that such does not exist in the world.
Bodhisattva Dharmā then asked Bodhisattva Ratnāgama:
“In transformation there is neither arising nor departing; who, then, is the master who brings it about?

Nirvāṇa is neither born nor extinguished, and it is not far from the five realms of existence. When one awakens the mind in the future and turns the wheel of Dharma, becoming pure and free from all defilements—who among all sentient beings is the one who delivers them?”
Ratnākara replied: "How excellent is this question!
Is it indeed for the purpose of severing the very root of all birth and death that you ask thus?"
Bodhisattvas possess nine kinds of Dharma-treasures:
first, regarding the transformer and the transformed, there is no master;
second, regarding nirvana and birth-and-death, from the very beginning there is no mutual cognition between them.
Third, regarding birth-and-death and cessation, there is neither cessation nor non-cessation;
fourth, among all the heavens, one does not return to birth, abiding in the place of non-birth;
fifth, whether the intention has already arisen or has not yet arisen, one dwells as it truly is.
Sixth, observing the three thousandfold world-system of Buddha-fields, one realizes there is no one to be delivered;
seventh, there is no place for thoughts to arise;
eighth, one causes all within the three thousandfold world-systems to attain nirvāṇa, yet feels neither joy in the mind when they do so, nor anger when they do not. Why is this?
Because all dharmas have no fixed location;

ninth, I cause all those who take up the path of Arhatship according to their vows to resolve their minds [for enlightenment]; if there are those who resolve their minds and seek such vows, I do not allow them to regress, nor do they give rise to further births, for there is no returning from their vow—these are the nine dharmas.
Furthermore, he spoke in verse:
"In the possible, there is no impossibility; In desire, there is no desiring.
That which is to be crossed over has no beholder; The Dharma turns where there is no permanence."
The wise have nothing to proclaim; because they cross over by means of non-going, they perceive the Great True Dharma, which is the most supreme thing in the world.
The Way has no constant name, and thus it is the treasure of the ten directions.
For one who has attained through non-attainment, there is no path within birth and death.
The four horses can never be exhausted, and the mind’s desires can never be satisfied;
the world delights in all these things, and by not relinquishing them, one does not attain the Way.
Those who fear existence have no liberation; those who do not fear it find no release.
One should designate the cycle of birth and death and establish it as the five destinies.
That which has retribution but no answer may be called this Dharma.
The Dharma is fundamentally non-dual; all truths are realized through awakening.
It is boundless and without limit, infinite and incalculable.
Its primordial state is like a shadow or an echo; there is no one who comes or goes.
In arising there is nothing that arises; for one who is free from all desires regarding phenomena, birth and death have no fundamental location, and the transformation of birth and death is thus.
In purity there is no purity; in defilement there is no defilement.
For the sake of all people in the ten directions, he cuts off the five realms of existence.
His pure mind is like water; it is entirely free from blemish or stain.
Whether blue, yellow, white, or black, he perceives the forms of them all.
All phenomena are beyond reproach; thus one attains the unsurpassed treasure.
As for the self and others, there is no one in the world who attains it.
Not abiding in the truth of non-abiding—such is the nature of all truths.
That which is awakened to is without anything seen; such is the truth of the world.
There is no one who crosses over, nor is there anyone who does not cross over; at all times in the world, who is there that does not exist?
Throughout the ten directions, those established in perfect awakening have all attained the unsurpassed treasure.
The Bodhisattva Dharma asked the Bodhisattva Ratnāgama:
"If one wishes to cause all the devas and people of the ten directions to spontaneously attain their respective proper places, what dharma must be practiced to achieve this?"
Ratnākara replied: "There are six things by which one attains this Dharma:
first, hearing and knowing that when this assembly gathers, that itself is the jewel."
Second, to hear this sutra is itself a treasure;
third, to attain fundamental merit is itself a treasure;
fourth, those who hear this Dharma of the sutra shall all obtain sixty thousand samādhis, which is itself a treasure.
Fifth, having already attained sixty thousand samādhis, one desires to inspire the aspiration for supreme enlightenment in the people of the ten directions; this is itself a treasure.
Sixth, one causes all those in the ten directions to gather beneath the Bodhi tree; this is itself a treasure.
When this sutra was being spoken, nine billion bodhisattvas and sixty-seven billion devas and humans all attained the state of the dharma-realm of non-arising;
nine hundred million bodhisattvas attained this samādhi.

The three-thousandfold great thousandfold Buddha-field shook in six ways; the devas in the sky performed great musical performances, and all the nāgas and asuras were able to hear and behold this profound samādhi.
Ānanda adjusted his robes, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is the name of this sutra?
How should it be upheld?"
The Buddha said to Ānanda, “This is called ‘Infinite Treasure’; you should uphold it.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the devas, humans, asuras, and non-humans were all filled with joy; each came forward to pay homage to the Buddha and departed.
The Sutra on the Samādhi of the Infinite Jewels Spoken by the Buddha, Scroll II.
